Learning about mercy through gentleness By Rev. Jim Hopkins Kate Bowler’s book Everything Happens For a Reason: And Other Lies I Have Loved is so worth reading that in April I decided to preach a three-sermon series based on it. Kate, a professor at Duke Divinity School and a respected researcher into the Prosperity Gospel, wrote the book after being diagnosed with stage four colon cancer. The sermons in my series were: April 8: “The Lie of Control” (Romans 8:26-28); April 15: “The Gift of Uncertainty” (Job 23: 1-17); April 22: “The Blessing of Gentle Words” (Matthew 5:7) In my first sermon I reflected on her words. “We love to tell ourselves that the world is ultimately fair. We try to convince ourselves that we can curate our lives, minimize our losses and stand on our own successes. We need to quit lying to ourselves.” The emphasis in the sermon fell on our understanding of Romans 8:28, the verse that many take to mean “everything happens for a reason.” I argued that the best way to read the verse is “in all things God works for those who love God” as opposed to “all thing work together for good for those who love God.” In the latter reading it seems is that everything that happens is ultimately caused by God. In the former reading God is at work with us, in the face of everything that happens, to bring about good. The former reading leads to a “Blueprint Theology” while the latter leads to a “Being-There Theology.” In my second sermon I noted that one of the pleas Kate makes to her well-meaning friends as she faced the possibility that she might not live to see her two year old son turn three was “Do not pour your certainty on my suffering.” In the biblical book of Job this is one of the central tensions. The suffering Job has lost everything and the only message his well-intentioned friends can deliver is “We know that suffering is the result of sin. You are clearly suffering so clearly you have sinned. Just repent and God will make you well.” They poured their certainty on his suffering with the result being that while they felt better, their suffering friend felt much worse. In the final sermon of the series the words of Jesus from his Sermon on the Mount were central: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy.” My theme was that when someone we love is suffering, a gentle word, a gentle touch or even a gentle silence can be a great mercy. Director provide updates at council meeting At the request of Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, Interim Fire Chief Despain and Recreation Director Putzer provided updates on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on their respective departments. The city has just completed a full year of restrictions. Updates were provided during a Monday night, March 1 City Council meeting. Fire Department Interim Fire Chief Micheal Despain offered an overview of vaccine availability in the county, and how residents can gain access to it. He also noted that if COVID-19 cases continue to drop, Alameda County can be moved to the less restrictive “Red Tier” as early as next week. “The [COVID-19] caseload is coming down considerably each and every week, and we could be changing into the Red Tier soon, which opens up a lot of options,” Despain said. Alameda County health officials should have enough data to make a determination as to whether or not the county will move into the Red Tier. If this happens, restrictions would be similar to “early November,” making indoor dining and gym access possible. Despain added that there is evidence of an expanded rollout of vaccine availability in Alameda County, though the actual number of vaccines administrated in the county hasn’t changed much. It is averaging about 15,000 doses per week. “As weeks go by, we’re seeing improvement. But what changed [in terms of availability] is that FEMA opened two mega-PODs [points of distribution] in California, and we’ve got one at the Oakland Coliseum,” he noted. articles.text: As the number of new coronavirus cases drop, Alameda County has hit all the metrics to enter a less-restrictive phase of reopening, but no change in status has been announced as of yesterday, Tuesday, March 2. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County has dipped to 2 percent as of Monday, March 1, its lowest point since early November last year. Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Several neighboring counties have moved out of the Purple Tier, including Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo Santa Clara, and Napa counties. They were moved into the Red Tier, which is the second-most restrictive tier in the state system. The adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people dropped to 6.3 in Alameda County, now below the 7 per 100,000 needed to move into the Red Tier. The case rate, positivity rate and positivity rate in the least advantaged census tracts all are meeting state guidelines to move into the Red Tier as of yesterday afternoon. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. After acknowledging that COVID-19 cases have plummeted compared to December and January, Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday that “we are seeing a little bit of a plateau, and one needs to be mindful of that.” No new cases of COVID have been reported in Piedmont in two weeks. The city has had 167 cases reported so far. Across Alameda County, 1,182 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, an uptick week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 80,780. There have been 25,075 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,705 cases in Hayward. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,481,611 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 52,497 deaths due to the disease statewide. Health experts remain concerned that more contagious strains of COVID-19 could spread in Alameda County. Variants first identified in South Africa, the United Kingdom and Denmark have all been discovered in the county, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention believe these variants spread more easily. This week, Alameda County officials reported a second case of a South African variant of COVID-19 known to be more resistant to certain vaccines. The cases are unconnected, and both were reported in individuals who had recently returned from international travel. The CDC believes both individuals were infected while overseas. “How is your corporate malaise coming along?”

articles.text: Newly approved Johnson and Johnson vaccine soon to arrive in California Over 17 percent of Piedmont’s adult population has been fully vaccinated against COVID-19 as of February 28, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Piedmont leads every other city in Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population by a wide margin. Over 38 percent of Piedmonters, some 3,213 people, have received at least one of the two doses needed for vaccination. Over the weekend, the Food and Dr ug Administration approved a vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson. This vaccine is the third approved by the FDA so far. On Monday, March 1, the pharmaceutical company began shipping out vaccine doses across the country. The ACPHD did not say when it would begin administering the first doses of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, but the state said the first doses would arrive this week. Because the Johnson & Johnson vaccine is only one dose, health experts hope that the addition of this vaccine will rapidly expand vaccination across the United States. On February 8, Alameda County began vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1, as defined by the state’s eligibility framework. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This group includes, for example, teachers and grocery store workers. This entire phase of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide. Alongside people in Phase 1B Tier 1, Phase 1A continues to be vaccinated. Director provide updates at council meeting By Allyson Aleksey At the request of Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King, Interim Fire Chief Despain and Recreation Director Putzer provided updates on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on their respective departments. The city has just completed a full year of restrictions. Updates were provided during a Monday night, March 1 City Council meeting. Fire Department Interim Fire Chief Micheal Despain offered an overview of vaccine availability in the county, and how residents can gain access to it. He also noted that if COVID-19 cases continue to drop, Alameda County can be moved to the less restrictive “Red Tier” as early as next week. “The [COVID-19] caseload is coming down considerably each and every week, and we could be changing into the Red Tier soon, which opens up a lot of options,” Despain said. By next Tuesday, March 9, Alameda County health officials should have enough data to make a determination as to whether or not the county will move into the Red Tier. If this happens, restrictions would be similar to “early November,” making indoor dining and gym access possible. Despain added that there is evidence of an expanded rollout of vaccine availability in Alameda County, though the actual number of vaccines administrated in the county hasn’t changed much. It is averaging about 15,000 doses per week. “As weeks go by, we’re seeing improvement. But what changed [in terms of availability] is that FEMA opened two mega-PODs [points of distribution] in California, and we’ve got one at the Oakland Coliseum,” he noted. There are expectations that the ease of access should increase actual distribution. The fastest way to get a vaccine, Despain said, is through your healthcare provider; then through the county health signup, and then myturn.ca.gov signup. You can be on all three of these “lists” at once. “Think of it as multiple routes – if your healthcare provider calls you and says ‘you’re up,’ you can go through that process, or through the county,” he added. “We caution people that it’s ok to sign up three times, but whatever ‘lane’ you get into, you get your shot, and stay in that See Covid Impact on page 30 More than 1/3 residents have received at least one vaccine dose Newly approved Johnson and Johnson vaccine soon to arrive in California By Barry Eitel Over 17 percent of Piedmont’s adult population has been fully vaccinated against COVID-19 as of February 28, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Piedmont leads every other city in Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population by a wide margin. Over 38 percent of Piedmonters, some 3,213 people, have received at least one of the two doses needed for vaccination. Over the weekend, the Food and Dr ug Administration approved a vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson. This vaccine is the third approved by the FDA so far. On Monday, March 1, the pharmaceutical company began shipping out vaccine doses across the country. The ACPHD did not say when it would begin administering the first doses of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, but the state said the first doses would arrive this week. Because the Johnson & Johnson vaccine is only one dose, health experts hope that the addition of this vaccine will rapidly expand vaccination across the United States. On February 8, Alameda County began vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1, as defined by the state’s eligibility framework. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This group includes, for example, teachers and grocery store workers. This entire phase of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide. Alongside people in Phase 1B Tier 1, Phase 1A continues to be vaccinated. This phase, comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of longterm care facilities, was the first group eligible when the first doses arrived in December. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County has dipped to 2 percent as of Monday, March 1, its lowest point since early November last year. Alameda County remains in the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric for reopening economic activity. Several neighboring counties have moved out of the Purple Tier, including Marin, San Francisco, San Mateo Santa Clara, and Napa counties. They were moved into the Red Tier, which is the second-most restrictive tier in the state system. The adjusted cases per day per 100,000 people dropped to 6.3 in Alameda County, now below the 7 per 100,000 needed to move into the Red Tier. The case rate, positivity rate and positivity rate in the least advantaged census tracts all are meeting state guidelines to move into the Red Tier as of yesterday afternoon. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. After acknowledging that COVID-19 cases have plummeted compared to December and January, Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday that “we are seeing a little bit of a plateau, and one needs to be mindful of that.” No new cases of COVID have been reported in Piedmont in two weeks. The city has had 167 cases reported so far. Across Alameda County, 1,182 new cases have been reported across the past seven days, an uptick week-over-week. The total caseload for the county is 80,780. There have been 25,075 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,705 cases in Hayward. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,481,611 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 52,497 deaths due to the disease statewide. Health experts remain concerned that more contagious strains of COVID-19 could spread in Alameda County. Variants first identified in South Africa, the United Kingdom and Denmark have all been discovered in the county, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention believe these variants spread more easily. This week, Alameda County officials reported a second case of a South African variant of COVID-19 known to be more resistant to certain vaccines. The cases are unconnected, and both were reported in individuals who had recently returned from international travel. The CDC believes both individuals were infected while overseas. articles.text: As reported in “City Asks County for 1 More Year to Create Affordable Housing Plan,” (February 3, 2021), the City of Piedmont is currently exploring ways to use its $2.2 million in Measure A1 funds from Alameda County to build affordable rental housing. Given the enormous crisis of housing affordability in the Bay Area, and in light of the history of discriminatory housing policies--from racial covenants to redlining--that restricted who could live in Piedmont for over half a century, we have an urgent responsibility as a community to create more inclusive, diverse, and affordable housing. We should look to build dwellings that will enable teachers, city staff, seniors, and families of diverse income levels to reside within our community. We are Piedmont residents who believe the city should strive to take full advantage of the Measure A1 funds. Our group includes affordable housing professionals, urban planners, architects, land use attorneys, and experts in urban history and policy. We bring more than 150 years of combined experience in these fields. At the February 1, 2021, City Council meeting, over a dozen Piedmont residents spoke in support of new housing in our community. Carol Galante, a Piedmont resident, Director of UC Berkeley’s Terner Center for Housing Innovation, and a former assistant director of HUD, urged the city to explore all available options. In addition to accessory dwelling units, Piedmont should explore the potential to create attractive apartments or townhomes along Grand Avenue, in the Civic Center, and at Blair Park, which would enable more family housing. The city should also look to update our zoning code to enable the creation of duplexes and incrementally denser and more affordable housing, as many cities throughout the country have already done. Rather than view new housing as having a negative impact on Piedmont, these changes can make our community even better. Given that the state is asking Piedmont to plan for nearly 600 new housing units as part of its next 10-year housing plan, an “all of the above” solution will likely be needed. Let’s take full advantage of the funds provided by Measure A1 and tackle the challenge by doing what Piedmonters do best: coming together and leveraging the extraordinary talent, expertise, and commitment to equity among our residents, leaders, and city staff. Let’s be a model for other small cities around the Bay Area in charting a progressive, innovative path towards meeting the housing challenge. We invite anyone interested in learning more about affordable housing to email us at piedmontracialequity@gmail.com. articles.text: Last year, there was a lot of attention on the Black experience in America, and one topic that must be included in that discussion is the impact of Black climate activists. Research shows that climate change does not impact all populations equally, and that Black communities face the negative effects of climate change more often than others. Due to this unequal burden, there is a long and important history of Black Americans leading the way on climate crises. This disparity can be seen in obvious ways, such as the infamous Flint, Michigan water and public health crisis, which impacted tens of thousands of people. Flint has a population that is over 50 percent African American, and the impact of the crisis on the community will be felt for decades. Another example is the Hurricane Katrina disaster, which killed over 1,000 people in New Orleans, a city which is 60 percent African-American. After Katrina, Black homeowners received $8,000 less in government aid than white homeowners because of housing value disparities. Predominantly black communities are more likely to be adjacent to landfills, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities. Black Americans are 40 percent more likely to have asthma than White Americans. These health outcomes are a direct effect of policy decisions that perpetuate unequal outcomes for different races in America. These health outcomes can be seen close to home. Oakland, which is 64 percent non-White, has childhood asthma rates of 18.3 percent. Compare this to Piedmont, which is approximately 75 percent white, and has child asthma rates of 12 percent. While mere miles apart, the discrepancies are vast. Black Americans, and particularly Black women, have been at the forefront of movements to make our environments a more equitable place to live for all. A local example is the Black Panther movement based in Oakland. Members organized drives to keep predominantly Black neighborhoods free of waste, hosting free health clinics and educating communities on the dangers of pollution. There now are groups in Oakland, throughout the Bay Area, and the state, that are focused on environmental issues, often helmed by Black people. One of these groups is the Climate Action Coalition in Oakland. The Coalition works on numerous issues, such as transit, food justice, and adaptation to climate change. Their overarching mission is racial and economic justice, which is directly related to climate solutions. Another group, Communities for a Better Environment, works in low-income Latino and African-American communities in Richmond and Oakland to address health hazards. Their goal is to prevent and reduce pollution and build healthy communities and environments. The California Environmental Justice Coalition (CEJC) is led by people of color and low-income communities. CEJC follows the principles of environmental justice and is committed to environmental, social, and economic justice. Thanks to these groups and many others, things can change for the better. Coupled with these organizations, municipal, regional, and statewide efforts can make a real difference to impacted communities. Keeping pressure on local policy makers can help make transportation, waste, and water systems more equitable for all people. Blackled movements in the community have historically made a difference and will continue to do so in the future. Nate Redinbo is the City of Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow in 2020-21. Call 420-3060 for more information (nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: Representative Eric Swalwell of Dublin introduced four anti-corruption bills on Tuesday, February 23, in response to the second failed impeachment of former president Donald Trump. The reintroduction is aimed to ensure that future presidents cannot “perpetrate some of the same corrupt acts,” Swalwell said. The bills would require that candidates, campaigns, and companies report any foreign interference in U.S. elections; enhance protections for ‘whistleblowers’ who come forward to expose official wrongdoing; and make it a criminal offense for the President, Vice President, or their families to enrich themselves from foreign sources. Swalwell, a member of the House Judiciary, Intelligence, and Homeland Security committees, previously introduced the bills between 2018 and 2020. “Donald Trump showed disdain for the moral and ethical norms we have always expected from an American president, so Congress must make sure these expectations are spelled out explicitly in law and are punished when violated.” “America needs these reforms to move ahead. We must make sure that these abuses can never happen again,” he said. The Duty to Report Act, which Swalwell introduced in June 2018 and April 2019, would closed sue for injunctive relief or monetary damages. Swalwell began drafting the bill after former President Trump and others attacked a whistleblower who raised concerns with the Director of National Intelligence’s Office of Inspector General about Trump’s actions in relation to Ukraine, which led to his first impeachment. “Republicans and Democrats alike for decades have agreed that threatening and trying to expose whistleblowers is wrong and undercuts long-established policy to encourage people to come forward with allegations of wrongdoing,” Swalwell said. “Trump’s actions showed our existing laws aren’t strong enough to protect whistleblowers’ right to anonymity.” The U.S. Constitution and current laws civilly prohibit government employees, including elected officials, but not their relatives, from receiving “emoluments” or gifts from foreign states, except as allowed by Congress. The Prevent Corrupting Foreign Influence Act, introduced by Swalwell in 2018, would expand the prohibition’s scope from merely gifts to include “anything of value.” “Unlike past Presidents, Donald Trump refused to adequately distance himself from his private business interests,” Swalwell said. “Americans deserve to know that their President is working for them and only them.” Photo by Getty Images East Bay Congressman Eric Swalwell impose a legal duty on federal campaigns, candidates, and political action committees (PACs) to report offers of assistance from foreign entities or nationals. articles.text: More and more high school graduates are taking time off before heading to college. An increasing number of students are choosing to take a gap year – a year off before beginning the college studies. A gap year may consist of educational and developmental activities while exploring the world, or looking into interests locally. Piedmont Parents Network hosted a conference on February 2 demystifying the concept of gap years and provided accounts of two 2020 Piedmont graduates, Ryan Tripp and Eliana Bloomfield. In some European countries as many as 30-35 percent of high school graduates take a gap year. Approximately 25 percent of students in Australia took a gap year even before the pandemic. Gap years became more common in Piedmont starting four years ago as families began embracing the benefits of a student taking a year off prior to college. The spiraling tuition costs of colleges contributed directly to some of the decisions to choose a gap year. As colleges went to online instruction last year due to the coronavirus epidemic, the gap year became an attractive option. Katherine Stievater, the founder of Gapyearsolutions. com, spoke at length during the Feb. 2 Zoom meeting on gap year possibilities. According to her research two to three percent of students in the U.S. took a gap year before the pandemic. But in the past year that number has tripled, with a total of 7-8 percent of incoming freshmen taking a gap year in the U.S. Eliana Bloomfield graduated from PHS last May and was accepted to Wesleyan University in Middletown, Connecticut. But in mid-July she switched gears and decided to take a gap year. articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

articles.text: OTR/L What is the best tool in my Occupational Therapy toolbox? If you were to ask my past and present students, the pink swing or Hedgie would likely be the top contenders. Having a suspended swing system is certainly a coveted sensory integration tool for occupational therapists, but it is not the best tool in my toolbox. Hedgie? He’s pretty darn cute and offers a soft option for a quiet space to calm and regroup. But he is not my best tool. The best tool in my toolbox is not an object or piece of equipment. Drum roll… The best tool in my toolbox, by far, is breathing. Conscious, mindful breathing. Truthfully, I had never pondered the question of which of my OT tools was the best. The question (and answer) occurred to me during a distance learning session with a kindergarten student. The recent transition to hybrid learning had been an exciting but dysregulating experience for this first-time student. Therefore, we began with a breathing exercise from the book Alphabreaths: The ABC’s of Mindful Breathing by Chris Willard and Daniel Rechtschaffen. S is for Superhero Breath Breathe in and imagine you are a superhero. Breathe out and imagine how you will help someone. How will you help someone? This has been a constant and troubling question for me over the past year, as I have had to navigate a new way to deliver services without many of the tools that I had come to rely on. At that moment, I realized that the answer was right in front of me, a kindergarten student practicing “S is for Superhero Breath.” I didn’t need the pink swing or Hedgie to support self-regulation. I had all that I needed even with the constraints of distance learning. Conscious breathing as an exercise has the power to reduce stress, calm, improve focus, in other words, self-regulate. Breathing exercises are a step toward managing emotions and behaviors and developing students’ self-awareness. Breathing is a superpower! The best part? Breathing exercises can be done anytime and anywhere. There is no age limit; however, the younger you start with your child the better. Begin teaching, modeling and practicing breathing exercises as early as preschool. Practice during periods of calm so that when needed, your child is ready to use the breath. Encourage, notice and name how they (and you) feel before and after. By teaching and modeling conscious breathing for your child, you will be providing them with a life-long tool for healthy self-regulation and ultimately success. How should you begin with the younger child? A great place to start is to read books together in order to build your child’s (and yours) toolbox. My recommendations include: • Calm with the Very Hungry Caterpillar by Eric Carle. A great book for preschool/TK students. • Breathe with Me: Using Breath to Feel Strong, Calm and Happy by Mariam Gates. Five simple breathing techniques for ordinary but challenging moments during the day. Watch and breathe with the author as she reads her book to elementary students on YouTube. It’s absolutely delightful. • Alphabreaths: The ABC’s of Mindful Breathing by Chris Willard and Daniel Rechtschaffen. Practice a fun and novel breath for each letter of the alphabet. I’d be remiss if I did not mention middle and high school students. You might be surprised to learn that your student has likely participated in some form of conscious breathing with their classroom teachers, especially over the last year. Start the conversation and ask them about it. What did they notice? When I include conscious breathing with tweens and teens, they report feeling calm, less stressed or simply “that was nice.” You know that you are onto something when a tween or teen answers a direct question with more than one word! Though I try to avoid recommending activities that require a screen, there are many popular guided breathAlphabreaths by Chris Willard and Daniel Rechtschaffen teaches children helpful breathing techniques. Calm with the Very Hungry Caterpillar by Eric Carle is a great book for preschool/TK students. ing lessons on YouTube as well as phone applications such as Headspace or MyLife. And for your taking the time to read this article to the end, here is my thanks to you. H is for Hugging Breath Close your eyes, Give yourself a hug, And gently breathe in and out. (Repeat 3 times) Feels nice doesn’t it? Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 3, 2021 BOOK REVIEWBETWEEN THE PAGES Stephen King’s The Gunslinger the start of 7 epic tales By Jay Russell Stephen King’s novel The Gunslinger initiates the unforgettable, must-read seven book epic series The Dark Tower. The Gunslinger introduces Roland of Gilead, a hero of classic westerns brimming with gruff stoicism and armed with cold steel. The hardened anti-hero of a stiff moral chivalrous code gets tossed into vivid and dynamic realms of science fiction. “The man in Black fled across the Desert, and the Gunslinger followed,” starts the saga. Roland Deschain, of King Arthur’s Knights lineage, chases the enigmatic but definitely maleficent Man in Black through a post-apocalyptic old west desert on a kamikaze mission. The Gunslinger’s odyssey intercepts the tale of Jake, a boy recently departed from “our” universe, as King’s dynamic multiverse begins to unfold. After crossing the desert, the hunt for the Man in Black takes Jake and Roland blindly through a tunnel called the Dark Chambers where The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger by Stephen King was originally published by Donald M. Grant, Inc. in 1982. they discover that “one could grow as hungry for light as for food.” Eventually, King unveils an impossible decision to be made between the life of an innocent and the pursuit of many lifetimes. The lingering aroma of macabre increases the suspense in all of King’s works, and readers do not have the comfort of knowing everything’s going to be okay. The fact that the “good guy” doesn’t have a free pass to survive in King’s stories injects them with realism, even when the tale lies firmly in fantasy (at time bordering on the insane). Aside from the potential impending doom, the series isn’t specifically in the horror genre. Librarians may choose to put the series under Western – or possibly Science-Fiction. More than anything The Dark Tower series enthralls readers. The stories are compelling, breathtaking, and a sterling example of originality. The 300-page length allows readers to test the waters of the entire 4,250-page series. Characters and universes from King’s other books interconnect with The Dark Tower, so reading it also serves as a portal to King’s entire collection. King labeled The Dark Tower saga as his Magnus Opus, his greatest achievement. He began The Gunslinger at the age of 22 in 1970 and it took him 12 years to circle back and finish the novel. The last installment of The Dark Tower was published in 2004, allin-all a 34-year enterprise. In contrast, you may want to avoid the 2018 movie called The Dark Tower, the horrendous botching of an entire legendary series of novels into a 90-minute advertisement for ineptness. No need to move your cursor onto the title on your streaming service. Just scroll past it, turn the TV off and enjoy your dark quarantine nights with The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger novel. articles.text: Troop 4 Scouts from Piedmont hike as the sun sets at Sibley. Scouts work on rope skills in Dracena Park. Despite difficult pandemic conditions, Troop 4 continues to provide a welcome social outlet for Scouts to engage with each other in outdoor community service projects, hikes and bicycle trips, and advancement activities, in addition to regular troop meetings via Zoom. Their outdoor activities are carefully calibrated to comply with the current County public health orders. In a range of other activities, Scout meetings in the future will feature discussions with a former Navy SEAL, an FBI agent and an Air Force pilot. Troop 4 has two new leadership roles, a Hikemaster and a Bikemaster, who regularly organize safe and socially distanced hikes and bike rides for Scouts. A hike led by Scout Mollie King was a unique sunset journey in Sibley Regional Park in Oakland. On a bike ride led by Scout Justin Katter across the Bay Bridge to Yerba Buena Island, Troop 4 Scouts were joined by former Beach Dads Club President Darrell Smolko and his two sons, for a beautiful afternoon of riding and camaraderie. “Kids are spending so much time on their screens with distance learning, we need to find a way to get them outside and physically active,” said Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. “One of the aims of Scouting is physical fitness, and the program is designed to be outdoors. It’s a perfect antidote to their current situation,” added Stokes, who regularly joins the Scouts’ outdoor activities. Troop 4 Scouts also meet periodically outdoors to develop advance Scouting skills, such as knot-tying and lashing. One Friday afternoon, Scout Bailey Cain helped teach younger Scouts how to lash sticks together properly. Troop 4 continues its commitment to community service. During the Scouting for Food Drive last Thanksgiving, they converted the annual food drive for the Alameda County Food Bank to online only. When they can engage in community service safely outside, they do so. Troop 4 Scouts recently did a clean-up project at Lake Merritt wearing masks and gloves, staying socially distanced, and using trash pickers. In anticipation of school reopening, in a community service project led by Scouts Matthew Lee and Bailey Cain, Troop 4 Scouts joined with Cub Scouts from Pack 4 and Girl Scouts from Troop 35521 to clean the Beach Elementary School garden on a sunny Sunday. “Troop 4 has always had a close community, but during the pandemic, our outdoor activities have been a real lifeline for the Scouts’ physical and mental health. Troop 4 finds ways to keep Scouts active & outdoors Despite difficult pandemic conditions, Troop 4 continues to provide a welcome social outlet for Scouts to engage with each other in outdoor community service projects, hikes and bicycle trips, and advancement activities, in addition to regular troop meetings via Zoom. Their outdoor activities are carefully calibrated to comply with the current County public health orders. In a range of other activities, Scout meetings in the future will feature discussions with a former Navy SEAL, an FBI agent and an Air Force pilot. Troop 4 has two new leadership roles, a Hikemaster and a Bikemaster, who regularly organize safe and socially distanced hikes and bike rides for Scouts. A hike led by Scout Mollie King was a unique sunset journey in Sibley Regional Park in Oakland. On a bike ride led by Scout Justin Katter across the Bay Bridge to Yerba Buena Island, Troop 4 Scouts were joined by former Beach Dads Club President Darrell Smolko and his two sons, for a beautiful afternoon of riding and camaraderie. “Kids are spending so much time on their screens with distance learning, we need to find a way to get them outside and physically active,” said Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. “One of the aims of Scouting is physical fitness, and the program is designed to be outdoors. It’s a perfect antidote to their current situation,” added Stokes, who regularly joins the Scouts’ outdoor activities. Troop 4 Scouts also meet periodically outdoors to develop advance Scouting skills, such as knot-tying and lashing. One Friday afternoon, Scout Bailey Cain helped teach younger Scouts how to lash sticks together properly. Troop 4 continues its commitment to community service. During the Scouting for Food Drive last Thanksgiving, they converted the annual food drive for the Alameda County Food Bank to online only. articles.text: Mackie McDonald backed up his impressive fourth-round run in the Australian Open with a championship victory at ATP Challenger Tour’s Forte Challenger 100 in Nur-Sultan, Kazakhstan from February 22-28. He picked up five very nice victories over host-nation’s Mikhail Kukushkin, Uzbekistan’s Denis Istomin, Frederico Silva of Portugal, Switzerland’s Henri Laaksonen, and Jurij Rodionov of Austria. McDonald walked into the ATP Challenger as the world’s No. 139 ranked player after picking up 53 spots from the Aussie Open, now vaulting another 21 positions to No. 118 following his title run in Kazakhstan. Mackie, 25, had his highest word-ranking of No. 57 at the time of his injury in April of 2019 when he sustained his torn hamstring tendon, to which he dipped to No. 132 around the time of his return in January 2020 and fell out of the Top 250 to No. 272 due to a length recovery. McDonald entered as one of two unranked Americans in the Kazakhstan Challenger, knocking off No. 1 seeded Kukushkin in straight sets 7-5, 7-5. Kukushkin was the hometown favorite and tournament’s only top-100 player at No. 96. Mackie dominated Kukushkin on the serve with seven aces and winning 72 percent of his first serves. His defensive prowess that shined in Australian Open wins against Borna Coric and Lloyd Harris carried over the Forte Challenger, scoring 39 receiving points and four break points. McDonald marched through No. 195 Istomin in the Round of 16 with scores of 6-2, 6-3, again with dominant defense with 27 receiving points and five of six break points gained. His toughest test came in the quarterfinals in a three-set contest against No. 179 Silva of Portugal, winning 6-4, 3-6, 7-6 (7-3). Both players had 11 aces and three break points, but it all came down to a heated seven point tiebreaker, where Mackie opened up 3-0, which included a beautiful crosscourt forehand for the third point. Silva battled back to 5-3, but a backhand volley approach shot and a Silva unforced error into the net was enough to seal it for the Pride of Piedmont. In the semifinals, McDonald faced the only other competitor who entered with a higher ranking than him, Laaksonen at No. 134, who was also the Challenger’s No. 5 seed. Mackie won handily in straight sets, 6-2, 6-1, recording six aces. Similarly, McDonald made quick work of No. 152 Rodionov 6-1, 6-2 on the way to the championship. He recorded seven aces, four break points, and 23 receiving points. Mackie was back at it this week in Nur-Sultan at the Forte Challenger 125. He defeated Canada’s Brayden Schnur in three-sets, 6-3, 4-6, 6-4 in the Round of 32 in the early hours of Tuesday, March 2.

articles.text: Piedmont MTB zwift avatar. It’s race day during the global pandemic. The peloton began to wind its way up the side of an active volcano, starting in mass at the same time, stretching out as the steepness of the road increased. Lava scaled down the mountain and rain started to fall in the cyclists’ virtual wonderland, Watopia, which is the oldest course on Zwift – a massive multiplayer online game and training program for cyclers and runners. This scene happened right here in Piedmont on a clear Monday night in the comfort of homes, garages, wherever they may be. The Piedmont Mountain Bike team has been using Zwift to train virtually over the winter, using its courses to stay in shape. Early in the season, the team decided to dedicate funds towards equipment required for a virtual setup for the whole team and now regularly have up to 18 riders at once on Zwift twice a week. To accomplish rides, standard bikes are set up on trainers with sensors and using a tablet or a computer to run the Zwift application. It’s like our own Peleton system, but more targeted towards cyclists and for a fraction of the cost. We are always connected via audio on Discord, chatting while we ride together in the game and seeing each other’s personally designed avatars. Piedmont MTB has been performing regular training workouts on Zwift since the beginning of December, led by Coach John Cheetham of Tempo Endurance Coaching. Since the Shelter in Place was lifted, we have been riding outside again and we are seeing very positive results. Those who have been training regularly on Zwift for the last three months are experiencing high levels of fitness that translates directly into the real world. We have also had a lot of fun with it, creating a source of connection for high school riders who have been sometimes isolated at home during this very strange time. We have created our own races, challenged each other to beat our personal bests, have caught up with each other and laughed together. As head coach I have “seen” the riders virtually three times a week, and it has been a great way for the coaches to build relationships with the team when we haven’t been able to see them in person. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is now officially in season, riding outside as well as virtually and still accepting new members. It is hosting the Piedmont Mountain Bike Classic from March 7-21, a socially distanced Strava segment challenge in Chabot. All local cyclists are welcome. For more information, see www. piedmontmtb.com/piedmontmtbclassic Sally Aldridge is coach of the PHS Mountain Bike Team

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s mountain bike team will host its first annual Piedmont MTB Classic race from March 7-21 and registrations are now open to the public. All proceeds will support the team, which receives no support from the high school or Piedmont Boosters because of its club status. The event will take place over a two-week period so that every racer can independently participate on their own time, thus making it a socially distanced, safe event. Each participant will record their times on designated trail segments using the Strava app, and prizes will be awarded for the fastest entrants in a number of categories: Middle School, High School, Adult and Overall. There will be two options for the race, the Short Course and the Long Course. The short course covers just over 9 miles of trail, and an elevation gain of approximately 900 feet. The Long Course covers 15 miles and 2,500 feet of elevation gain. The cost to participate is $40 per rider. Race proceeds will be used to purchase a team trailer to help transport equipment to season races It will be dedicated to Lynden McLaughlan, a team coach who passed away unexpectedly in 2019. To learn more about the race and the team, go to www.Piedmontmtb.com.

pages.text: 14 Wednesday, March 3, 2021 PHS Mountain Bike Team cycling virtually through pandemic Piedmont MTB zwift avatar. By Sally Aldridge It’s race day during the global pandemic. The peloton began to wind its way up the side of an active volcano, starting in mass at the same time, stretching out as the steepness of the road increased. Lava scaled down the mountain and rain started to fall in the cyclists’ virtual wonderland, Watopia, which is the oldest course on Zwift – a massive multiplayer online game and training program for cyclers and runners. This scene happened right here in Piedmont on a clear Monday night in the comfort of homes, garages, wherever they may be. The Piedmont Mountain Bike team has been using Zwift to train virtually over the winter, using its courses to stay in shape. Early in the season, the team decided to dedicate funds towards equipment required for a virtual setup for the whole team and now regularly have up to 18 riders at once on Zwift twice a week. To accomplish rides, standard bikes are set up on trainers with sensors and using a tablet or a computer to run the Zwift application. It’s like our own Peleton system, but more targeted towards cyclists and for a fraction of the cost. We are always connected via audio on Discord, chatting while we ride together in the game and seeing each other’s personally designed avatars. Piedmont MTB has been performing regular training workouts on Zwift since the beginning of December, led by Coach John Cheetham of Tempo Endurance Coaching. Since the Shelter in Place was lifted, we have been riding outside again and we are seeing very positive results. Those who have been training regularly on Zwift for the last three months are experiencing high levels of fitness that translates directly into the real world. We have also had a lot of fun with it, creating a source of connection for high school riders who have been sometimes isolated at home during this very strange time. We have created our own races, challenged each other to beat our personal bests, have caught up with each other and laughed together. As head coach I have “seen” the riders virtually three times a week, and it has been a great way for the coaches to build relationships with the team when we haven’t been able to see them in person. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is now officially in season, riding outside as well as virtually and still accepting new members. It is hosting the Piedmont Mountain Bike Classic from March 7-21, a socially distanced Strava segment challenge in Chabot. All local cyclists are welcome. pages.text: Wednesday, March 3, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON Cascades of the South Fork of Tuolumne River Outside Groveland are Rainbow Pools, 1.4-mile hike By Jonathan Comeaux The Post has a hidden treasure for you this week in Stanislaus National Forest. Let’s say you couldn’t land a camping spot inside Yosemite National Park and were aching to see thriving rivers and powerful waterfalls. Outside Groveland on the way to Yosemite on Highway 120 is a short 1.4 mile out-and-back (2.8 mile roundtrip) hike along the South Fork of the Tuolumne River that has four magnificent waterfalls. Opposite Rainbow Pools, a popular summer swimming hole, is a descending trail that currently is almost completely free of other hikers during these cool winter months. You’ll be hard-pressed finding a better hike of less than three miles. The unnamed trail starts at 2,884 feet in elevation, dropping to 581 feet while walking alongside the river. We passed just six people on a Saturday. It you’re accustomed to hiking inclined trails, like the ones found in the Oakland and Berkeley hills, this trail is comparable. Your eyes will be glued to the river. The view gets better and better on your hike. The waterfall furthest upstream is 25 feet tall. The Middle Fork’s cascade is estimated at 182 feet and forms a confluence with the South Fork. Staff Photos Continuing down the path leads to the third waterfall, a powerful 45-foot cascade that drops into a large pool. A trail along the South Fork of the Tuolumne River provides a short walk with four magnificent waterfalls. Pictured here are a pair of falls where the Middle Fork (left) and South Fork (right) meet. Your eyes will stay locked on the rushing waters to your left, with views that improve with every step, it seems. After a mile, a pair of impressive falls are seen a mere hundred feet from each other. The first is around 25 feet tall that drops into a large pool, a place where swimmers would be in the summer. Continuing on the path toward the bridge is the Middle and South Fork Confluence, where the Middle Fork of the Tuolumne River ends with an estimated 182-foot-tall cascade that merges with the South Fork. Hikers can take in the sheer size and force of the falls by standing next to the small pool at the base, while the bridge provides a clear glance at both falls to your left and right. After another short walk around the bend is another glorious 45-foot waterfall. It’s worth noting that you’ll be passing through an area with warning signs of potential rockslides. The trail continues to a concrete viewing area and a stairwell that leads closer to the river. Pack a lunch and enjoy it here before traveling back to your car. While resting at the base of the stairs we noticed what looks to be a fenced-off former mining shaft, which has thick-metal wiring lining over the river to an opposite shaft entrance. Traveling down to the river gives a clear look of the South Fork. You can see the former base of a bridge that connected the two shafts. To reach this location, there is an off-road parking area shortly after passing the bridge which spans the South Fork of the Tuolumne. Follow the paved path, which reads Forest Rte 1N07 on GPS devices, taking the gravel trail that emerges on your right after 0.4 mile. Be wary of an area of rockslides near the third waterfall. The path leads down to the river, where you can spot the last waterfall, also around 25 feet tall. A view of the South Fork of the Tuolumne River with a platform of a former bridge in the face of a rocky cliff.

articles.text: For 25 years I’ve walked all around the San Francisco Tribal & Textile Art Show – eyes dazzled, spirit awakened, brain and heart stimulated, aesthetic sense challenged – until my feet ached. The Fort Mason Pier felt like my homey museum, my eyes were so happy, but the damn concrete floor made my feet ache. I loved seeing and studying – and sometimes buying – audacious artworks from ancient and fascinatingly cultures different from mine. As an art lover, collector at heart and art dealer, every February the Tribal Show and the Indian Show were the winter’s highlights. I always showed a double booth full of African and Oceanic art in the Tribal Show, and a medium booth of Pre-Columbian art in the Indian Show. I’d sell a lot, buy a lot, talk a lot, even listen to the old collectors who are my old friends. As I see it, this is Our Year of Adaptation. This year’s Tribal Show which I love, just opened and runs through Wednesday midnight. This year it is online – a virtual show. May I suggest that if you love art, take a virtual trip to exotic foreign cultures from your armchair and see stunning examples of art from Africa, Oceania, The Americas, and Tribal Asia. Before it closes tomorrow night at midnight, click on: https://www. virtualtribalandtextileartshows. com /cms/product- categor y/ dave-deroche-art-of-africa-oceania-the-americas/ Ceremonial Dance Mask. Lwalwa tribe. D.R. Congo. A striking, dramatic example of innovative artistic abstraction in African art, which modern artists like Picasso, Braque, and Vlaminck ‘borrowed’ from heavily in ‘inventing’ Cubism. Offered by Dave DeRoche in the Virtual/Online SF Tribal Art Show for $6000. Leave your passport behind. No traffic. No parking problem. No ticket line. And no cost. What could be better? Stay in your bathrobe if you wish. Travel with your eyes. Imagination, personality, and wisdom. Traditions and soul are built right into the object that catches your eye. Ask questions of the exhibitors. They’re lonely this year, too. Learn from them. They love their art objects and they would love to tell you about them. They might even sell them to you so they can acquire something new for themselves. For more information, see: https://www.virtualtribalandtextileartshows.com/

articles.text: Museum to reopen with U.S. debut of Calder-Picasso Exhibit The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco have announced the reopening of the de Young Museum this week. It is scheduled for members on March 4 and 5, and to the general public this Saturday, March 6. Visitors will be excited to not only return to the museum, but to see the U.S. debut of an exhibit with works of Alexander Calder and Pablo Picasso. The exhibit includes more than 100 paintings, sculptures, drawings, and photographs that explore the relationship between Calder and Picasso, largely regarded as two of the most influential artists of the twentieth century. The exhibition Frida Kahlo: Appearances Can Be Deceiving has been extended through May 2, and is available for ticket reservations. Uncanny Valley: Being Human in the Age of AI has also been extended through June 27 and is available with a general-admission ticket. The de Young Museum and the Legion of Honor are maintaining rigorous health and safety measures based on county guideDigital programming In addition to reopening the de Young in Golden Gate Park on Saturday, the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco have announced a series of virtual programming through summer 2021, to include community partnerships with renowned artists, historians, musicians and activists. All museum programming will be offered in digital form through June 2021. A new partnership between Alexander Calder (left) and Pablo Picasso, two of the best-known names in 20th-century art, share a number of striking similarities in artwork - all on display in the Calder-Picasso exhibition. [photo courtesy of Musee National Picasso-Paris] San Francisco’s deYoung Museum in Golden Gate Park. lines. Visitor capacity is reduced to 25 percent, and timed tickets are required. To obtain tickets, visit https://deyoung.famsf.org/ exhibitions. the Fine Arts Museums and the SeeBlackWomxn collective will launch a five-part series focused on the contemporary Black Arts scene. The collective was founded by artists and activists Tahirah Rasheed, Angela Hennessy, Dana King, and Jamani Montague, and celebrates the lineage and legacy of Black women in contemporary arts. SeeBlackWomxn will serve as a collective narrative of artists and writers who contribute to Black feminist theory. The platform emphasizes self-representation and aims to stray from the stereotypical tropes assigned to Black women and identifying women. The series is programmed through the museums’ “Virtual Wednesdays” and Local Voices podcast, which aims to explore the impact of public art on the Bay Area community. This year, notable artists contributing to the podcast include Lava Thomas, Catherine Wagner, and Alison Saar, musical duo Mercury Soul, Fredrika Newton of the Huey P. Newton Foundation, the #SayHerName Movement, Susan Cervantes of the Precita Eyes Muralists, artist duo Rue Bainbridge, artist and composer Gryphon Rue, and artist Peter Simensky. articles.text: Cal Shakes will host a virtual fundraiser on Friday, March 26, entitled “Lights Up!” It will feature Artistic Director Eric Ting, Managing Director Sarah Williams, and Bay Area artists for an evening devoted to raising funds to get artists back to the stage once again. The virtual celebration will serve as “a love letter to classic stories and the extraordinary people that make them come to life.” The event will be a night of fun and celebration, joy and laughter, and a moment to come together in support of the resiliency of the arts. Cal Shakes started as an artistic collective in 1973, and became an official company – Berkeley Shakespeare Festival – at John Hinkel Park in 1974. Over the past 40 years, Cal Shakes has become a cornerstone and mainstay of Bay Area Theater, producing works from the Shakespeare canon and beyond. In 1991, the company built the Bruns Amphitheater in the hills of Orinda. Visit https://calshakes.org/ lightsup/ to register for the fundraiser.

articles.text: Tabla master Zakir Hussain San Francisco Symphony has added a new episode of “Currents,” which explores the intersection between classical music and Indian classical music and culture. articles.text: Kate Winslet and Idris Elba star in the thrilling survival story, The Mountain Between Us Movie review by Chris Honoré The Mountain Between Us is a title offering a nifty summary of what this film is about from it’s opening set-up to the last frame. Of course, it uses a familiar template but is still solidly entertaining with two superb actors. Briefly, and trying to avoid touching on acts two and three, Dr. Ben Blass (Idris Elba) and Alex Martin (Kate Winslet) meet by chance at the Boise, Idaho airport. Their flight, they are told separately, has been cancelled. He is desperate to get to Denver and then Baltimore where he will, as a neurosurgeon, perform a lifesaving operation. Alex, a photojournalist, is looking for a way to get to Denver in time to complete the final preparations for her wedding that is scheduled for the following day. They agree to charter a plane for the trip to Denver. The pilot is an old timer (Beau Bridges) who brings his golden lab along and who rides in the second seat. All goes according to plan (speaking of plan, guess who forgot to file one?) until there is a riveting, breathtaking crash that occurs on a harrowing stretch of a snow-covered mountain range. It’s January and the weather is unforgiving. In effect The Mountain Between Us is two stories. The first is one of survival that is reminiscent of The Revenant. The cold is penetrating. The odds are against them. The decision to be made is, should they stay with the crash site and hope that the homing beacon in the tail section of the twin-engine plane is working, or take as much gear as possible and try and hike out. One impediment to that plan is that Alex has suffered a severe leg injury. The second story embedded in this tale of survival against all odds is the relationship between Alex and Ben. Almost from the outset the audience knows that despite the stress of their situation there is a palpable attraction. Of course, their consuming priority is to do all that is physically possible to prevail against their overwhelming circumstances. But still… Movies of this type never fail to resonate with me. Once the film has begun, I’m in it for the full hour plus change. And though the story may seem somewhat incredible, Winslet and Elba do a masterful job of keeping the narrative moving forward on both levels. One small spoiler: the dog survives the crash. The Mountain Between Us. Starring Idris Elba, Kate Winslet and Beau Bridges. Directed by Hany Abu-Assad. 1 hr., 40 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré “Raped while dying.” “And Still No Arrests” “How come, Chief Willoughby?” On a side road outside of Ebbing, Missouri, Mildred Hayes (Francis McDormand) has rented three billboards, and each possesses one of the lines above, painted in black on an attention-getting red backdrop, asking the seminal question regarding solving the rape and murder of her daughter: “How come?” It’s been seven months since her daughter was murdered and Mildred has decided that the Chief of Police, William Willoughby (Woody Harrelson) has had more than enough time to find the killer. The signs are her protest. And so begins what was one of the best films of 2017. It is a dark and tragic comedy that is not in any way a murder mystery. Rather, it is a character study of how three individuals react to the demand, posed by Mildred, for an investigation, and more importantly, an arrest. Though Mildred has made her statement, she is nowhere close to being finished. For her, the billboards are just act one. This narrative is not a police procedural. Three Billboards is something else entirely and takes the expectations of the audience in a totally different direction. Think of it as a cultural autopsy of a small, fictional heartland town. At the center of this film, at its essential core, is Mildred, trapped between grief and rage. She crosses line after line with her anger until the town, which was once sympathetic because of her loss, turns against her. The Chief is much cared for and he makes every effort to convince Mildred that he has done all that is possible to find the killer of her daughter. Mildred of course is not satisfied. To make the film even edgier is the Chief’s second in command, a surprisingly dim deputy, Jason Dixon (Sam Rockwell), known for his racism and abuse of authority. He lives with his mother and regards his badge as a license to do just about anything he pleases. In some strange way his anger mirrors that of Mildred but for very different reasons. That he wears a uniform defies understanding, especially considering the compassionate persona of Willoughby, a family man (two daughters) and a lovely wife. Three Billboards is a study of personal demons and regret and courage. It is irreverent, a tsunami of revenge, yet a web of moments of kindness that surprises. All the minor characters that satellite the Chief, Mildred and Dixon are outstanding in their verisimilitude. Most, especially Mildred, are consistently scatological, dark and ragged at the edges, unforgiving – and yet forgiving. It should be no surprise that this film won two Academy Awards – for McMormand as Best Female Actress, and Rockwell as Best Supporting Actor. A note: I have done my best to say as little as possible about the plot, while avoiding describing any scenes in detail. Three Billboards should be seen fresh, allowing the twists and turns to catch the audience by surprise, and to enjoy its creative quirkiness. But realize that it is steeped in moments of violence that appear and then vanish like so much mist. Once again: this film is stunningly well acted; it’s raw and ambiguous; and, finally, redemptive. Well, sort of redemptive. But in the end the audience is asked to decide. Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. Directed by Martin McDonagh. Starring Francis McDormand, Woody Harrelson and Sam Rockwell. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated R. Frances McDormand stars in Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.

articles.text: Hailee Steinfeld stars as Charlie in Bumbleebee. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Transformers film franchise made its debut in 2007, followed by four sequels, each directed by Michael Bay and each, incrementally, shredding the original charm and solid story telling. Bay seemed content to indulge his predilection for CGI chaos, over-the-top histrionics, explosions, and bot slams. In every way the recently released Bumblebee (a prequel) is not only redemptive, but resurrects that sweet spot mined by Shia LaBeof, as Sam Witwicky, in the first Transformers when he negotiates with his dad for a car. He finds a hard-used, yellow Camaro on a lot and convinces his dad that this rusty ride works for him. And so his adventure begins. Ditto Charlie Watson (Hailee Steinfeld), who is on the cusp of turning 18 and declares that, like Sam, all she wants is a car. Any car. After a brief lead-in segment where the Autobots/Optimus Prime and the Decepticons/Megatron are locked in a destructive battle on Cybertron, their home planet, the narrative shifts to 1987. The place is the San Francisco Bay Area. Charlie is grieving for her father who died two years before of a heart attack while they were restoring a vintage Corvette that still sits in the garage. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around the junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday, he tells her), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is a classic and wondrous reveal. As she is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the benign-looking VW transforms and there standing before her is a huge banana yellow bot. It’s a meet cute scene that ends with a startled, at-first-disbelieving Charlie naming the Transformer Bumblebee. As she learns, he proves to be a gentle, even timid, giant. And after catching her breath, she and B.B. tentatively bond. Actually, as it turns out, both, in a way, are hiding out – though for B.B. the stakes are much higher. They begin what proves to be a touching friendship. It’s at this point in the story that Charlie’s adventure begins. This is a relationship story. Even when the Decepticons locate Bumblebee (who we learn from the initial set up that he is on a mission for Optimus Prime), the film doesn’t drop off a cliff into vacuous violence that became the brand for the five sequels. Bumblebee is a genuinely good movie that engages and entertains. It’s perfect for those tweens and newbie teens who likely don’t have a clue what life was like in 1987, but understand what it feels like to discover a bot in their home garage. The film comes along at Christmas time, and beckons to parents and kids alike to spend two hours with this Hasbro endorsed tale that has the iconic E.T. embedded in scene after scene. It is distinctly a user-friendly family film. Bumblebee. Directed by Travis Knight. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, John Cena and Pamela Adion. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Before discussing the most recent Star Trek incarnation, consider the following: Star Trek Beyond is the 13th movie in a 50-year-old franchise which also includes six TV series and some 100 million books and comics sold during the last half century. Star Trek is now a cinematic senior citizen and this fact begs the question: why? What is there about these films – about these characters who spend most of time encapsulated in a large Frisbee with enormous thrusters – that sets them apart from other franchise films? Is it because they dare to go where no travelers have gone before, into the final frontier – space? It’s a remarkable pop culture phenom (now rebooted), supported by countless Trekies, some covert others nostalgically closeted, but all fans of the premise. Beyond perhaps offers up an answer as to why. This film, like most of its predecessors, is a solid, straightforward adventure story, packaged in 23rd century technology (much of it dreamy and ersatz but still cool, like, say, a phaser on stun). There is a heterogeneous crew, always a merciless villain. In the case of Beyond he’s a biped E.T. with a very bad complexion named Krall (Idris Elba), intent on putting the Federation astronauts in sustained jeopardy. In the initial set up, the Enterprise receives a distress call from a stranded ship and is lured by Krall into an ambush that turns out to be a swarm of metal “bees,” meaning tiny weapons that look like a hundred thousand starlings rising, turning and then attacking. Why the attack is initiated has something to do with an Abronath, which holds the key to ultimate power, and is coveted by Krall, who, by the way, is one very bad dude. When the Enterprise crashes on said planet, that’s when the games begin. It’s one set piece after another of hyper-action, with Captain Kirk (Chris Pine) and Spock (Zachary Quinto), along with their crew fighting for their lives. A new character, Jaylah (Sofia Boutella), is introduced as one of the lone rebels fighting Krall. She’s fresh and resilient and interesting with kind of a goth, white-face, zebra-stripes look. The nuts and bolts, carried out with spectacular ingenuity, consist of old machinery (an ancient starship) made serviceable; new machinery that breaks down and is repaired; Spock, injured, is healed plenty pronto by Bones (Karl Urban); and all this is buttressed by a still functional oldtimey transporter. The fan base will be satisfied. The newbies don’t need to get caught up because Beyond stands on its own. If you’re inside the tent with the franchise and ready to suspend your disbelief, then go happily where countless fans have gone before. Star Trek Beyond. Starring Chris Pine, Zachary Quinto and Zoe Saldana. Directed by Justin Lin. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated PG-13. articles.text: He was famous; but he wanted to be a composer. His name was Lionel. Lionel Blythe. He was really famous. So were his younger siblings. His younger brother, John, was so famous that all you had to say was “the profile“ and everybody knew who you were talking about. His sister was famous, too. Of course, you don’t know them by Lionel Blythe, John Blythe and Ethel Blythe. Somewhere along the line the entire family changed its name. When I tell you that the name they chose was Barrymore, you probably think you know where I’m going with this story. But you are wrong. You see, Lionel Barrymore never wanted to be an actor. He was coerced into acting by the rest of the family. Lionel Barrymore’s talents lay in other areas of the arts. I guess he became an actor simply because it was the easiest way to make a living. But he really wanted to be a composer. He came to music rather late in life. I think his first piano lessons were at the age of 17. But he went to Paris to study art. He was a very good artist, and you can buy some of his artwork on e-Bay. I became interested in the music of Lionel Barrymore because I first heard him as the host on a famous “Concert Hall“ program. He introduced the great violinist Jascha Heifetz. Soon after that I found out that Lionel Barrymore was a very enthusiastic composer. His music impressed me. But he was a modest guy and didn’t push his music nor did he pull rank in any way. The first piece of his that I heard was a musical memorial to his brother, John Barrymore, in 1942. The performance was by the Philadelphia Orchestra conducted by Eugene Ormandy. It was a tone poem of scope and profound musical sensitivity. Some music critics took cheap shots at Lionel Barrymore’s music. They accused him of being too conservative. Perhaps they confused his music with his support of Thomas Dewey over FDR. His art was also conservative. In this he shares a kinship with Velasquez. It all depends on how you view the artist and his work. But if we analyze Lionel Barrymore‘s music, we must conclude that he continued a wonderful American tradition of composers. He was very friendly with Edward MacDowell – and no one denigrates MacDowell. So, music lovers, go onto the Internet and listen to some of the music of Lionel Barrymore. Just imagine: he could have written the musical scores for his own movies and be respected like two Lionel Barrymore famous composers, Max Steiner and Erik Wolfgang Korngold. A look at Center for the Arts The sphere of music makes many connections. This was driven home to me last week with the news about a classic Victorian home in San Francisco being moved to a new location a few blocks away. Maybe you saw it. The Englander House was justifiably famous, but not only because it was a classic Victorian. Its interior boasted those mysterious gaslights which were in the famous Hollywood movie of the same name, Gaslight. I played many concerts in the Englander Mansion when I was concertmaster of the San Francisco Concerto Orchestra. This orchestra was a noble venture. It showcased the talents of the finest musicians from every orchestra in the area. The repertoire consisted entirely of concertos. The gaslights were extinguished, and the orchestra died a slow death. Why? The musicians supported the venture wholeheartedly, but the press ignored the venture completely. So did the politicians in San Francisco. I see some similarities to our beautiful city of Piedmont, where the Piedmont Center for the Arts has been the cultural gem of our city for some 10 years. We hear people asking about diversity, but the incontrovertible fact is that the arts are colorblind. No one can tell the religion, the race, or the gender of any performer by listening. Likewise, it is not possible to identify the political stance of a performer. All you have to do is look at all orchestras, choruses, opera companies and dance companies. All you see wherever you are is diversity. But artists and musicians rarely talk about it. Art, after all, is based upon talent regardless of a person’s origins or race or gender. The Piedmont Center for the Arts, which enjoys a sterling reputation throughout the Bay Area, is the city’s cultural gem. Without it, Piedmont is just another bedroom community.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok A ham and sweet potato strata is a lovely brunch during springtime. Spring brunch time is nigh, and this “strata” features the classic pairing of ham and sweet potatoes. Technically the method here doesn’t layer the ingredients (a strata), but over the years I’ve found the layering process doesn’t make a big difference in the end result. So, I opt for an easier preparation. If you feel inclined, you can layer the ham-sweet potato-onion mixture with slices of bread and cheese, then pour the milkegg mixture over all of it. Or go with the simpler version here and mix everything together in a big bowl and transfer it to the baking dish. This is an excellent vessel for leftover meats and vegetables. As with many of my recipes, pandemic or not, this one is flexible on ingredients and flavorings. Eggs, half-half, and bread are the basis upon which you build, with additional ingredients that influence the resulting dish. I happened to have a package of ham steak and leftover roasted sweet potatoes, which are the basis here. Kale is a staple at our house. If you enjoy this recipe, check out my blog for Piedmont Brunch, using sausage, zucchini and bell peppers. Ham and Sweet Potato Strata INGREDIENTS • 4 ounces bread, cut into 3/4” cubes, about 3 - 4 cups • 1 - 2 teaspoons olive oil • 12 ounces fully cooked ham, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 - 2 cups cooked sweet potato, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 medium bunch kale, sliced crosswise in 1/2” wide strips, about 2 - 3 cups • 1 cup yellow onion, diced • 5 extra-large eggs • 2 cups half and half • 1 teaspoon dry mustard powder • • • • Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Pinch of cayenne pepper, to taste 5 ounces jalapeno jack cheese, shredded, about 1 cup 1/4 cup green onions, thinly sliced for garnish PREPARATION Preheat the oven to 350˚. Place bread cubes on baking sheet. Bake for 10 - 15 minutes, until dry and firm. Remove from oven and let cool. Heat olive oil in a large skillet on medium heat, add onions and cook stirring frequently, until they become soft and translucent. Add sliced kale and continue cooking until the kale has just barely wilted. Remove from the skillet and transfer to a large mixing bowl, at least 3-quart size. In a medium mixing bowl, combine the eggs, whole milk, grated cheeses, dry mustard, salt and pepper. Make sure the eggs are fully scrambled within this custard mixture. Add the ham and sweet potations, kale and onions; then stir until evenly mixed into the custard. Fold in the toasted bread. Pour everything into a well buttered, 2-quart baking dish. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least four hours, up to 24 hours. When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 350˚. Remove the plastic wrap from the dish, place it on oven rack in the middle position in the oven. Bake for one hour or until fully set. Test by inserting a clean knife into the center of the dish. If it comes out clean, the custard is set. It should be nicely browned and puffy; and pulling slightly away from the sides of the dish. It will settle as it cools, so know that the gorgeous puff is fleeting. For more information or to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok at PiedmontPantry.com.
