You may be pleased to learn that March 29 is National Mom and Pop Business Owners Day. You might not necessarily think of your business as a “Mom and Pop” operation, but it certainly contributes to the well-being of your family now, and possibly to that of future generations, too – if you make the right moves. Depending on the nature of your business, you may have spent the past several months more concerned about today than tomorrow, given the serious economic repercussions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still placing stress on a great many business owners across the country. If your business has been adversely affected by the pandemic, you might be eligible for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan. As you may know, recent legislation provided $285 billion more for this program. To learn more, and to start the application process, visit the Small Business Administration website at www.sba.gov. You have until March 31 to apply for a PPP loan. Other relief also may be available. But regardless of whether you apply for one of these loans, you can take other steps to help maximize the benefits you get from your business – and perhaps even extend its longevity. Here are a few suggestions: • Establish a retirement plan. If you don’t already have a retirement plan, it’s never too late to set one up. As a business owner, you have several options, including an “owner-only” 401(k), a SIMPLE IRA and a SEP-IRA. All these plans are fairly easy to establish and can offer potential tax advantages, as well as providing you with a source of retirement income in the future. You may want to work with a financial professional to pick the right plan for your needs. • Coordinate your business assets with your investment portfolio. Like most business owners, you may have a great deal of your personal wealth tied up in your business. And, as the past year has certainly shown, this can be risky. Consequently, you’ll need to weigh this risk factor when deciding on investing in your retirement plan or in other investment accounts. This doesn’t mean you should try to avoid all risk only by pursuing the most conservative vehicles – which would be counterproductive to achieving enough growth to meet your retirement income goals – but you will need to pay close attention to your investment mix to ensure it provides you with an appropriate balance to what you’ve invested in your business. • Develop a transition strategy. How will you make the transition from business owner to the next phase of your life? Will you sell the business outright? Will you gradually transfer it to a family member? If so, what mechanism will you use? It’ a good idea to have these types of plans in place well before you need to enact them, so you may want to consult with your financial, legal and tax advisors soon. A “Mom and Pop” business may sound quaint and carefree – but, as you know, running a business of any size can be an all-consuming endeavor and always involves significant financial concerns. So, I opt for an easier preparation. If you feel inclined, you can layer the ham-sweet potato-onion mixture with slices of bread and cheese, then pour the milkegg mixture over all of it. Or go with the simpler version here and mix everything together in a big bowl and transfer it to the baking dish. This is an excellent vessel for leftover meats and vegetables. As with many of my recipes, pandemic or not, this one is flexible on ingredients and flavorings. Eggs, half-half, and bread are the basis upon which you build, with additional ingredients that influence the resulting dish. I happened to have a package of ham steak and leftover roasted sweet potatoes, which are the basis here. Kale is a staple at our house. If you enjoy this recipe, check out my blog for Piedmont Brunch, using sausage, zucchini and bell peppers. Ham and Sweet Potato Strata INGREDIENTS • 4 ounces bread, cut into 3/4” cubes, about 3 - 4 cups • 1 - 2 teaspoons olive oil • 12 ounces fully cooked ham, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 - 2 cups cooked sweet potato, cut into 1/2” cubes, about 2 cups • 1 medium bunch kale, sliced crosswise in 1/2” wide strips, about 2 - 3 cups • 1 cup yellow onion, diced • 5 extra-large eggs • 2 cups half and half • 1 teaspoon dry mustard powder • • • • Salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste Pinch of cayenne pepper, to taste 5 ounces jalapeno jack cheese, shredded, about 1 cup 1/4 cup green onions, thinly sliced for garnish PREPARATION Preheat the oven to 350˚. Place bread cubes on baking sheet. Bake for 10 - 15 minutes, until dry and firm. Remove from oven and let cool. Heat olive oil in a large skillet on medium heat, add onions and cook stirring frequently, until they become soft and translucent. Add sliced kale and continue cooking until the kale has just barely wilted. Remove from the skillet and transfer to a large mixing bowl, at least 3-quart size. In a medium mixing bowl, combine the eggs, whole milk, grated cheeses, dry mustard, salt and pepper. Make sure the eggs are fully scrambled within this custard mixture. Add the ham and sweet potations, kale and onions; then stir until evenly mixed into the custard. Fold in the toasted bread. Pour everything into a well buttered, 2-quart baking dish. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least four hours, up to 24 hours. When ready to bake, preheat the oven to 350˚. Remove the plastic wrap from the dish, place it on oven rack in the middle position in the oven. Bake for one hour or until fully set. Test by inserting a clean knife into the center of the dish. If it comes out clean, the custard is set. It should be nicely browned and puffy; and pulling slightly away from the sides of the dish. It will settle as it cools, so know that the gorgeous puff is fleeting. Recently, HDR Remodeling completed a bathroom refresh in a guest bathroom in Oakland and we’re sharing how we made it happen. Our clients came to us with a request for a makeover of their guest bathroom with a contemporary design. They loved the charm of their 1920s-era house but wanted to liven up this space. In the original bathroom, the toilet sat in the center of the room and was the first thing guests saw as they approached. The fixtures and finishes were also of the original 1920s era. The driving factor of our design was to maintain the existing architectural details of the house, while infusing our client’s personal style – a blend of modern and vintage – with an appreciation for unique natural handmade materials. We collaborated closely with our clients who wanted to incorporate an organic and natural form of wood into the bathroom. That became the source of our inspiration and a focal point for the bathroom. Open shelving and natural elements also create a sense of openness in tight spaces. Bathroom before refresh. Bathroom refresh with natural countertops and bold backsplash. Because our goal was to remain within the footprint of the existing bathroom, we had to be creative with the space we had. We shifted the layout of the bathroom, repositioning the original bathtub and relocating the toilet using a wall-mounted tank behind the door. This gave us additional valuable square footage and made space for the statement piece of the bathroom - a custom wood countertop and shelves sourced from our client’s family member, Revival Woods of Kapa’au, Hawaii. To add dimension, we built a deep tub ledge for seating and to hold bathing necessities. A bold patterned tile adds interest to what would otherwise be a simple, tiled wall. By not changing the square footage, we were able to keep costs down and allowed for some major changes to upgrade this bathroom. Incorporating intentional fixtures and key finishes is pivotal in transforming a small space and giving it new life. articles.text: Photo by Amber Brumfiel Dark pink buds are starting to appear on the bare branches of Piedmont’s Eastern Redbud trees. The groundhog may have seen its shadow this year, but spring is in the air as you look at the flowering trees in Piedmont’s urban forest. There are beautiful examples all around town, including the cluster of Eastern Redbuds (Cercis canadensis) that greet you at the entrance to Witter Field and Piedmont Park at the intersection of Wildwood and Prospect Avenues. Nominated by former resident Lisa Kieraldo, these cheerful trees were designated as Heritage Trees in 2019. Dark pink buds are just starting to appear on the bare branches of these trees. Considered long lasting, the showy blossoms will last for a few weeks once they fully bloom. Green leaves will then start to appear. The Eastern Redbud is the state tree of Oklahoma. This deciduous tree has heart shaped leaves and some varieties around town have stunning fall colors that add to their enjoyment as small garden trees. The Eastern Redbud is sometimes referred to as the Spicewood Tree because its bark and green twigs are sometimes used as seasoning for wild game. The Piedmont Park Commission is accepting nominations for 2021 Heritage Trees through March 19. The Heritage Tree program is an opportunity for Piedmont to recognize its distinctive trees. The community is invited to nominate trees growing on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. Nominated trees will be considered based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. The chosen trees will be announced at the Park Commission hearing on April 7 and honored at this year’s virtual Arbor Day celebration on April 30. To nominate a tree visit the City’s website, http://www. ci.piedmont.ca.us/ and complete the downloadable form. For more information, contact Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov (510- 420-3064). Amber Brumfiel is a member of the Piedmont Park Commission.

articles.text: Dear Abby: Have you found out anything new about COVID-19 and our pets? Can we spread it to them? Too young to be vaccinated yet, –Jordan and Fat Cat Dear Jordan and Fat Cat: Here’s what I found on the CDC’s website on February 10, 2021: • We do not know the exact source of the current outbreak of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), but we know that it originally came from an animal, likely a bat. • At this time, there is no evidence that animals play a significant role in spreading SARSCoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, to people. • Based on the limited information available to date, the risk of animals spreading COVID-19 to people is considered to be low. • More studies are needed to understand if and how different animals could be affected by COVID-19. • We are still learning about this virus, but it appears that it can spread from people to animals in some situations. • People with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 should avoid contact with animals, including pets, livestock, and wildlife. Hope this helps calm Fat Cat’s concerns, –Abby Dear Abby: With all these pet adoptions, we are having trouble finding a trainer to help us with our new adopted boy, Elvis, the cutest dog ever. Any ideas? Perplexed and pooped, –Eve, Jacob & Elvis Dear Eve, Jacob and Elvis: This is the tricky side of pet adoptions. Trainers are booked up teaching dogs how to live with their humans. Give Heidi Kistler a call of Pawsitively Pampered Pets in Oakland, 510-336-9861. I’m not sure what she and her husband Ryan have available but at the very least, she may be able to add Elvis to a dog walking group which helps any dog with socializing and adhering to basic commands. Heidi also walks and takes care of a lot of Piedmont dogs and can help if you start to travel to allocation where Elvis can’t join you. Can’t wait to meet Elvis. Can he sing? –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: Diane (Di) Paulhamus Anderson, a lifelong resident of Piedmont, passed away at her St. Helena home on February 24 after a short illness. She was 88. Above all, Di was a loving wife, devoted mother and grandmother and an exceptionally generous friend. Invariably, she was the first to reach out to a family member or to one of her countless friends if they were in any sort of need. It is remarkable how many of Di’s friendships extended through two, three and more generations of families. Di was also a forceful presence, getting what she felt was best for those close to her. She was always in charge in the most positive of ways; very little got past her. Di was born June 3, 1932 in Seattle to Dwight Randolph Paulhamus and Eleanor Jackson Paulhamus. They were a pioneering Puyallup Valley family and among the founders of the Washington State Fair. Her paternal grandfather, W.H. Paulhamus was a Washington state senator. As a child, Di and her family moved to Piedmont where she would reside for the rest of her life. It was at Piedmont High School, class of 1950, where she started dating her future husband, Jack Blair Anderson. Di attended the University of Arizona and was a member of the Delta Gamma sorority. Returning to the Bay Area, she started working in the personnel department for Kaiser Corporation, and resumed her romance with Jack. Di and Jack were married February 11, 1956 and enjoyed a love affair for the following 62 years. Their three children, Ellin, John and Michael were raised in Piedmont and attended public schools there. Jack passed away in 2018. For nearly 40 years, Di and Jack divided their time between Piedmont and St. Helena. In addiDiane P. Anderson, a lifelong resident of Piedmont and a consummate hostess, died on February 24 at her home in St. Helena. She was 88. tion to allowing Di an additional home to decorate, St. Helena gave her the opportunity to extend her circle of friends to the wine country. A consummate entertainer, Di was known for countless parties, most notably her blacktie Christmas Eve celebration in Piedmont and New Year’s Eve luncheon in St. Helena. Di’s sense of taste and style extended from her homes to her personal fashion. She knew what she liked to wear and carried it off with the gracious assertiveness that exemplified her life. Few, if any women, could rock leopard prints, leather pants and boots up to the age of 88. Di and Jack traveled the world with their family and friends. This included joining Jack on his favorite fishing trip to the wilds of British Columbia, where Di not only caught salmon, but looked marvelous doing so. Her travels invariably took her back to the places she loved most, including Lake Tahoe. There was no better moment than to be with Di at Tahoe during “mauve time” with your favorite cocktail. Late in life, Di developed a taste for premium tequila, which she drank by the shot to the refrain, “Arriba, Abajo, Al Centro, Pa’dentro.” For obvious reasons, this ritual endeared Di to a new generation of younger fans. Di was incapable of sitting still. Mostly, she channeled her considerable energy helping her family and friends. She also made time for various entrepreneurial pursuits, including hosting art shows and running a catering business. Catering proved to be challenging as most guests preferred being in the kitchen with Di where the real party was happening. Di recalled visiting the famous Rancho La Puerta Spa some 55 times, embarrassing scores of much younger women with her fitness as she dragged them up and down the mountains of Baja, California. Di is survived by her children, Ellin Anderson Purdom and husband Ned, John Blair Anderson and wife Liz, and Michael Dwight Anderson. She is survived by four grandchildren, Ted Purdom (Lluisa), Charlie Purdom, Jack Anderson, and Caroline Anderson; and great granddaughter Apollónia Purdom Escandell. She is also survived by her sisters-in-law, Ellin Firth and Barbara Anderson, nieces Catherine Hughes and Elizabeth Simonetti; and grandniece Jane Simonetti and grandnephew Peter Simonetti. Di and Jack were married February 11, 1956 and enjoyed a love affair for the following 62 years. Their three children, Ellin, John and Michael were raised in Piedmont and attended public schools there. Jack passed away in 2018. articles.text: Dear Jim: We are planning a basement renovation project but have been struggling to find the right person for the job. It seems most contractors, architects and engineers we’ve been referred to are booked months in advance. Also, preliminary prices are higher than we expected. Is this also your experience, and how would you suggest we move forward with our remodel? As I’ve mentioned in previous articles, residential remodeling and repair are being highly affected by current world events and economics in a way that is significantly impacting contractors and their clients. Since the changes may have a major effect on your timelines and budget, it is important that you understand their potential impact on projects you are now considering. Huge demand for home live/ work spaces Most of the clients we are currently working for have moved their “headquarters” home and concepts relating to “remote” work have contractors adapting to this move toward home-based work/living spaces. In addition to keeping staff safe, it is becoming evident that decentralizing the office is also a cost-effective model for the modern work world. As a result, a need for new living and recreation space, storage, home offices, and basement units has increased substantially, thus directly affecting all lead times for home remodeling businesses, including designers, subcontractors, architects, and engineers. With backlogs currently the norm, and people becoming more aware of the defects in their homes or simply wanting to eke out more space, supply and demand is putting pressure on the home renovation industry. Prices have increased dramatically. Additionally, Coronavirus-induced mill shutdowns along with a booming housing market have led to huge increases in lumber costs. For example, plywood sheathing costs (one of our biggest purchases) have doubled in the last year – from $20 a sheet to around $40. As a consequence, wood-based manufactured products affected by shutdowns, such as windows and doors, have also seen spikes in cost. Concrete and steel are also seeing price jumps, but not as dramatic as the lumber industry. Labor costs have increased as well, with skilled employees and laborers demanding higher wages and jumping ship to other companies due to labor shortages and high demand for their services. One striking example of these inflations are when potential customers I gave estimates to 2-3 years ago return ready to begin a project, requiring me to reprice the project with increases averaging around 30%. Building Departments struggle to keep up. Another pressure of getting a project started but with long delays is the process of permit approvals, which is different city by city. Even before Covid, permitting, particularly with remodeling projects, involved planning, zoning and extensive plan checking. It is not uncommon for contractors to have to wait 4-6 months for permits on more extensive jobs in certain cities (not Piedmont, of course). Simple repair jobs which I used to be able to have permits issued the same day or in a few days and over the counter, are now subject to a lengthier process, creating challenges in getting projects off the ground. In Berkeley, for example it can take me 3-4 days to get the cashier to respond to an e-mail request to pay for a permit that is ready to issue, something which in the past could have been resolved with a 5-minute phone call. For a while I thought that the lack of distractions for home-based workers might actually improve efficiency, but I now believe the lack of personal face-to face interaction can make things more complex. Some cities are still relying on video inspections, which can be slow and challenging with poor internet connections. Supply-chain issues significantly impacted Other reasons for delay are ongoing problems with the manufacturer, shipping and delivery of products. We are currently working on a large home remodel and many items are often out of stock, with lead times on the building of doors, windows, cabinets etc. often doubled or tripled. Even basic, mass produced items, like IKEA cabinets, are constantly out of stock. We’ve been waiting months, along with other contractors, to gather a few at a time as they become available. Certain production facilities and specialty shops have closed down completely. They are working with reduced staffing and report difficulty procuring raw materials. Shipping is slowed, and even paying more to expedite delivery is often impossible. Items are regularly arriving weeks behind scheduled delivery dates, shoving dates for starting, completing, or continuing projects all over the calendar. Final word The bottom line is that your construction project may not only be more expensive than expected, but also due to the numerous pressures outlined above, it may be difficult to find a contractor right away. My best advice is to anticipate this as a new reality, even as Covid potentially wanes. More efficient systems may be slow to return, and contractors will continue to be very busy, especially if the economy improves and working at home becomes more of a staple. Be sure that you plan your project well in advance, and have proper expectations about costs and a time frame for completion to avoid the pitfalls associated with construction in 2021. articles.text: Havens’ Avenue of Palms was for sale in 1922. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. articles.text: Mention of honey bees provokes a variety of responses. The buzz of a bee and the contrasting yellow and black colors inspire thoughts of golden honey. They incite fear of the sting. And they symbolize our dependency on pollinating insects. Whatever thoughts come to mind, keeping bees can be a fascinating connection with the wildness we find around us. Although bees live in painted rectangular boxes, they are still wild insects. They forage for their food and propagate on their own. Opening a hive of honey bees is like opening a window to the wildness we can find even in the city. This time of year, a hive is small but growing. Most of the nectar and pollen collected is used to raise more bees. The nectar provides the carbohydrates; pollen is the protein source. Honey bees literally work themselves to death and live only six weeks during the busy season. The queen bee is no slouch either. She can lay more than her body weight in eggs in a single day. Despite the independence of bees, a beekeeper must still tend them. Those stacks of white boxes grow taller through the spring to give the colony more room to store honey and more room for bees. If a colony senses that its home is full of bees and honey, it will swarm. The name sounds scary and the sound of a swarm of honey bees is scary. I have heard sevThe white powder on the head and thorax of the bee is pollen from a Rosemary blossom. Beekeeper Nils Kaufman next to one of his hives. eral in recent years pass over my house. They are loud. But in reality, the honey bee is most docile during a swarm. She has no home to defend and is looking for one. She does not want to sting. In fact, honey bees are bred for gentle behavior. If you see a swarm of bees cluster on a branch or under the eaves, call a beekeeper. If possible the beekeeper will collect the bees and give them a new home. I have done this wearing a T-shirt and shorts; the bees are very calm. Compared to other backyard agricultural pursuits such as gardening or raising chickens, beekeeping does require some specialized knowledge but much less time. Beekeepers check on their bees every two weeks during the spring and summer, and less frequently in the fall. The population of bees decreases in the fall. They do not want more mouths to feed than necessary, but they do need enough bees to cluster and stay warm. The biology of these fall bees changes as well to allow them to survive several months of winter. The biggest threat to honey bees is the varroa mite, in Latin, varroa destructor. There are organic treatments that kill these mites, and with care, varroa are little more than a nuisance. Piedmont is an almost ideal place to raise bees. A hive or two in the backyard is not a bother as long as there is sufficient space and adequate care. The reward? The honey harvested will be as prized as any home-grown tomato. In addition to supporting novice beekeepers, Nils Kauffman has played bagpipes for the high school and Piedmont Scout events. For more information, contact him at: nils.j.kauffman@ gmail.com.

Recent videos of attacks in Oakland and San Francisco – caught on residential and commercial security cameras – have circulated online and on social media. Even with this blatant evidence, however, a victim’s refusal to report an assault or burglary can hinder investigations. “These [victims] will tell me about an attack or robbery, but they are unwilling to share that with the authorities. They tell me they’re afraid of retaliation, and they also feel that since it has already happened, what’s the use in reporting,” Chan explained. Chan noted that he has worked closely with both Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley, and the Oakland Police Department (OPD), to address underreporting concerns. Chan acknowledged that both offices are aware that underreporting is an issue. In a press conference in February, newly-appointed Oakland Police Chief LeRonne Armstrong said that the reported data on Asian-targeted hate crime incidents do not reflect the actual number of incidents because many altercations go unreported. In addition, the City of Oakland has slashed $15 million from the department’s overtime spending, which Chief Armstrong said is hampering the department’s ability to “keep the peace.” It is also hampering the department’s ability to respond to victims who do report. Some victims have waited hours for police to arrive after reporting a burglary or assault, mentioned Chan. “When the incident happens, and the perpetrator has left, it no longer becomes a priority,” he said. Officers will encourage victims to file a report online, but that can present language barrier issues. Chan said he understands that the Oakland Police Department is stretched thin with its budget cuts. Community members across the Bay Area have recognized this, too, and have offered to help protect vulnerable communities. Volunteers have offered to patrol the streets of Chinatown in an effort to deter physical violence, robberies, and vandalism, with offers of help coming from as far away as Stockton and San Jose. A fundraiser, with a goal of $80,000, was initiated by Oakland resident Joanna Au on gofundme.com to hire armed patrol security guards for Chinatown merchants. It surpassed its goal within 24 hours. “When we are seeing so many bad things happening, we’re also seeing good deeds from the community, and residents coming to support us,” Chan acknowledged. “We understand that this is a sensitive issue, and we understand the calls to defund the police [departments].
